__dirname.summary: `__dirname` is a CommonJS module-local string containing the directory of the currently executing script. Each module, including dependencies, receives a value based on its own location.
__dirname.explanation: In a CommonJS module, `__dirname` is a module-local string containing the directory of the file currently being executed. Each module receives its own value, so a dependency resolves its directory rather than the directory of its importer.
__dirname.returns: String containing the directory of the currently executing script.

useCases.scenario: Locate assets or configuration without depending on the process working directory.

useCases.title: Handle module-local paths
useCases.scenario: Distinguish the directory of a dependency from that of its importer.

Its value belongs to the current module, not to the entire Node.js process.
A dependency gets a directory based on its own file location.
gotchas: Treat it as module-scoped rather than as a universally shared global value.

__filename.summary: __filename is a CommonJS module-scoped string containing the current module's absolute file path, with symbolic links resolved. Each module receives its own value.
__filename.explanation: In a CommonJS module, __filename is a module-scoped string containing the current module's absolute path after symlinks are resolved. Each module receives its own value, so dependencies see their own file paths rather than the caller's path.
__filename.returns: A string containing the current CommonJS module's absolute filename, with symlinks resolved.

example.title: Inspect the current module path
example.code:
console.log(__filename);
console.log(__dirname);
example.explanation: Prints the current CommonJS module's absolute filename and its containing directory.

useCases.scenario: Logging or diagnostics

useCases.title: Build an absolute path relative to the current file

useCases.title: Distinguish the caller's file from a dependency's file
useCases.scenario: Inspecting dependency locations

keyPoints: __filename identifies the file containing the currently executing CommonJS module.
Its value is an absolute path, and symbolic links are resolved.
The value is local to each module, including dependencies.
Node.js supplies __filename as part of the CommonJS module environment.
gotchas: Do not assume the value exactly matches the path spelling used to start Node.js.

AbortController.summary: AbortController signals cancellation to selected Promise-based APIs. Call abort() to activate its signal and optionally provide a reason.
AbortController.explanation: Create an AbortController, pass its signal to a supported Promise-based API, and call abort() to notify that operation. The controller exposes the signal; abort() can optionally record a reason, and the signal emits an abort event that consumers use to stop or reject work.

parameters.name: reason
parameters.description: Optional cancellation reason, retrievable from the associated AbortSignal's reason property.

example.title: Cancel a fetch request
example.explanation: This runnable example cancels a fetch request when the timer calls abort().

useCases.title: Timeout cancellation
useCases.scenario: Cancel fetch or another supported Promise-based operation when a deadline expires.

useCases.title: Cooperative shutdown
useCases.scenario: Stop ongoing asynchronous work in response to user or application shutdown.

useCases.title: Group cancellation
useCases.scenario: Share one cancellation signal with multiple operations that should stop together.

keyPoints: AbortController coordinates cancellation for selected Promise-based APIs.
Its design follows the web-platform AbortController API.
Call abort(), optionally supplying a reason for the cancellation.
The optional reason is available through the associated signal's reason property.
Calling abort() activates the signal and emits its abort event.
Listeners receive the abort event when the controller is aborted.
gotchas: An associated signal emits the abort event only once, so a controller cannot be reused to signal multiple cancellation cycles.

AbortSignal.summary: AbortSignal communicates cancellation to selected Promise-based APIs through an EventTarget-compatible signal. Controllers and static helpers can trigger cancellation immediately, after a timeout, or when any of several signals aborts.
AbortSignal.explanation: AbortSignal is an EventTarget-based cancellation signal used by selected Promise APIs. A controller can trigger it, while static helpers create an already-aborted signal, a time-based signal, or a signal composed from several signals; listeners can inspect aborted and reason.
AbortSignal.syntax:
class AbortSignal extends EventTarget
AbortSignal.abort([reason])
AbortSignal.timeout(delay)
AbortSignal.any(signals)

parameters.name: reason
parameters.description: Optional value explaining why the signal is already aborted.

parameters.name: delay
parameters.description: Milliseconds before the signal is aborted.

parameters.name: signals
parameters.description: Signals to combine; the resulting signal aborts when any provided signal aborts.

AbortSignal.returns: Static helpers return AbortSignal instances; the signal exposes aborted, onabort, and reason properties.

example.title: Abort an operation with a reason
example.explanation: Creates a signal, observes its one-time abort event, and aborts with a custom reason.

useCases.title: Cooperative cancellation
useCases.scenario: Cancel an in-flight fetch or other Promise-based operation when a user or system requests shutdown.

useCases.title: Timeout enforcement
useCases.scenario: Set a maximum duration for an asynchronous operation.

useCases.title: Composed cancellation
useCases.scenario: Accept cancellation from several independent sources, such as a request, timeout, or application shutdown.

keyPoints: It communicates cancellation from an AbortController to interested observers.
AbortSignal.abort(reason) creates a signal that is already cancelled and can carry a reason.
AbortSignal.timeout(delay) provides cancellation driven by a millisecond delay.
Consumers can react to cancellation by listening for the abort event.
The reason property exposes the value supplied when cancellation occurred.
gotchas: Use a one-time listener because the associated controller triggers the abort event only once.
AbortSignal.timeout() aborts after the specified delay; choose the delay in milliseconds.
With AbortSignal.any(), the reason comes from the signal that first causes abortion.

AsyncLocalStorage.summary: AsyncLocalStorage stores request- or operation-scoped state and makes it available across asynchronous callbacks and promise chains. Create a context with run() or enterWith(), then read it with getStore().
AsyncLocalStorage.explanation: AsyncLocalStorage associates a store with an asynchronous execution context. Start a context with run() or enterWith(), then retrieve its store from callbacks and promise continuations created within that context.
AsyncLocalStorage.syntax:
new AsyncLocalStorage([options])
asyncLocalStorage.run(store, callback[, ...args])
asyncLocalStorage.enterWith(store)
asyncLocalStorage.getStore()
asyncLocalStorage.disable()

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Optional configuration object; its defaultValue property supplies the value used when no store is provided.

parameters.name: store
parameters.description: Value supplied as the context store, available through getStore() within the context.

parameters.name: callback
parameters.description: Function executed in the context established by the instance.

AsyncLocalStorage.returns: The constructor creates an AsyncLocalStorage instance; getStore() returns the current store or undefined outside an initialized context; run() returns the callback's return value.

example.title: Propagate request context across async work
example.explanation: The request identifier remains available across the asynchronous timer callback created inside run().

useCases.title: Request tracing
useCases.scenario: Attach request IDs or correlation metadata to logs without passing them through every function.

useCases.title: Per-request identity
useCases.scenario: Keep authenticated user or tenant context available throughout asynchronous request handling.

useCases.title: Observability
useCases.scenario: Propagate tracing spans and diagnostic metadata across promise chains and callbacks.

keyPoints: The class preserves contextual state across asynchronous operations.
Instances have separate contexts, so their stores do not interfere.
run(store, callback) executes the callback with the supplied store and returns the callback result.
Async work started inside run() inherits that callback's store.
enterWith(store) activates a store for the rest of the synchronous turn and subsequent asynchronous calls.
getStore() retrieves the store associated with the current execution context.
gotchas: getStore() returns undefined when no context was established with run() or enterWith().
A store supplied to run() is scoped to its callback; code outside that callback cannot access it.
Creating an instance alone does not establish an active store.

Blob.explanation: The global Blob class stores immutable raw data assembled from strings or binary parts. Its size and MIME type are available synchronously; arrayBuffer(), bytes(), text(), and stream() provide asynchronous or streaming access to the content, while the original data remains safely shareable across worker threads.

The constructor combines all supplied parts in order into one Blob.
The size property reports the Blob's byte length.

stream() exposes Blob content through a ReadableStream.

arrayBuffer() returns copied data rather than a view into the Blob's internal storage.
Worker messaging can share a Blob without immediate transfer or copying; copying occurs when arrayBuffer() or text() is called.

Buffer.summary: Buffer represents fixed-length sequences of bytes in Node.js. It extends Uint8Array and is widely used by Node.js APIs for binary data.
Buffer.explanation: Buffer is Node.js’s fixed-length byte sequence type. It extends Uint8Array and provides constructors and methods for encoding, copying, inspecting, and transforming binary data used by many Node.js APIs.

Buffer.alloc creates initialized storage of the requested size and can fill it with a value.

child_process.summary: The node:child_process module runs operating-system subprocesses from Node.js. Its asynchronous APIs avoid blocking the event loop, while synchronous variants block until completion.
child_process.explanation: The node:child_process module creates and manages operating-system subprocesses. Use spawn for asynchronous execution with streamed input and output, spawnSync for blocking execution, exec or execFile when collecting completion results, and fork for another Node.js process with IPC.
child_process.syntax:

spawn(command, args?, options?)

parameters.name: options

ClientRequest.summary: http.ClientRequest is the writable stream representing an in-progress HTTP client request. It is returned by http.request(), accepts request data and headers, and emits the server response when response headers arrive.
ClientRequest.explanation: ClientRequest is the writable stream returned by http.request() while an HTTP request is in progress. Configure its headers or write request data, listen for the response and errors, then call end() to complete a request that has no more body data.

interview.question: How does the module support large HTTP messages?
interview.answer: Node's HTTP interface avoids buffering an entire request or response, allowing large or chunked messages to be streamed. This reduces the need to hold complete payloads in memory.

interview.question: What is the purpose of Node.js's `node:path` module?
interview.answer: The module supplies utilities for working with file and directory paths. The default implementation uses the conventions of the operating system running Node.js, and it can be imported with either CommonJS or ES module syntax.
interview.followUp: How would you process POSIX paths consistently on Windows? Use `path.posix`, which exposes the POSIX-specific implementations.

interview.question: What does `path.join()` do?
interview.answer: `path.join()` combines path segments with the platform-specific separator and normalizes the resulting path. It is useful for constructing a path from pieces without manually inserting separators.
interview.followUp: How does `resolve()` differ? It produces an absolute path, using the current working directory when the supplied segments do not establish one.

interview.question: How can a relative path between two paths be calculated?
interview.answer: `path.relative(from, to)` returns the relative path from one location to another, based on the current working directory. It performs path computation rather than checking the filesystem.
interview.followUp: What should be used when the required result must be absolute? Use `path.resolve()` to resolve a sequence of segments into an absolute path.

gotchas: Methods such as basename and dirname disregard trailing separators, which can affect the returned final component or directory.
Do not rely on the default path behavior for portable POSIX-format data; select the POSIX implementation explicitly.

interview.question: What are the four fundamental stream types?
interview.answer: A Readable supplies data, a Writable accepts data, a Duplex supports both directions, and a Transform is a Duplex that modifies data as it passes through. These abstractions let applications process data incrementally.
interview.followUp: How would you connect stages while handling completion and errors? Use pipeline-style stream composition rather than manually coordinating every write, and select the callback or promises utility API according to the surrounding control flow.

interview.question: How does a Readable expose available data?
interview.answer: Streams are EventEmitter instances, so readable streams can notify application code when data is available. Data can also be consumed through other documented readable-stream mechanisms, including piping and async iteration.
interview.followUp: Why prefer incremental consumption for large inputs? It avoids requiring the complete input to be held and processed as one value, allowing work to proceed as chunks arrive.

interview.question: How do you access the stream module and its promises API?
interview.answer: The module can be loaded with `require('node:stream')`, and its promises API is available through `require('node:stream/promises')` or `require('node:stream').promises`. The promises API provides asynchronous stream utilities that return Promise objects instead of using callbacks.
interview.followUp: When is the promises API especially convenient? It fits naturally inside async functions, where completion and failure can be handled with `await` and ordinary Promise control flow.
